summary.business: Max Healthcare Institute Limited operates a network of 21 healthcare facilities across 11 cities in India with over 6,000 beds, delivering tertiary and quaternary care across specialities including oncology, cardiac sciences, neurosciences, orthopaedics, renal sciences and organ transplantation. Beyond hospitals, the Company extends its care ecosystem through Max Lab (pathology and diagnostics) and Max@Home (home healthcare and wellness services), and serves international patients through Patient Assistance Centres across multiple countries.

currentContext.strengths: Scale as India's most valuable listed healthcare organisation, with an integrated network of 21 facilities and 6,000+ beds across 11 cities|High network utilisation — 76% occupancy in FY2025-26, with ~73% of beds located in metro markets|Asset-light, scalable growth model combining owned/operated hospitals, subsidiaries, managed facilities and Partner Healthcare Facilities (PHFs)|Advanced clinical technology base — 42 robotic surgical systems (including Da Vinci platforms) and the EDGE radiosurgery system, supporting complex, high-acuity procedures|International patient network via 12 Patient Assistance Centres across multiple countries plus 5 partner offices, supporting medical value travel demand|Governance recognition — IiAS 'Next Leader' for the second consecutive year (top 20 in S&P BSE100 for corporate governance) and inclusion in the NIFTY 50 Index|Growing AI/digital capability built on a multimodal longitudinal electronic health data repository, applied across the patient journey (symptom search, pre-OPD assessment, discharge summary optimisation, health-record analysis)
currentContext.strategies: Multi-pronged growth approach: expanding capacity organically, scaling through asset-light models, and pursuing disciplined inorganic growth initiatives|Capital allocation framework emphasising disciplined growth, balance sheet prudence and return-accretive deployment of capital; intends to maintain net debt-to-EBITDA at not more than 2.5x|Prioritise high-return brownfield expansions and asset-light opportunities, while selectively pursuing greenfield projects in attractive catchments with compelling demand fundamentals and clinical talent availability|Inorganic growth pursued with strict valuation, integration and return thresholds|Strengthen advanced quaternary care capabilities across high-demand clusters through a balanced mix of brownfield, greenfield and asset-light capacity additions, phased to align with demand visibility|Broaden access beyond hospital walls through the rapidly growing asset-light Strategic Business Units, Max@Home and Max Lab|Build an ecosystem of evidence-based, scalable AI solutions leveraging a growing repository of multimodal longitudinal electronic health data, deployed across the patient journey|Deepen commitment to research and academics through MIME/MIAPE (education) and the Office of Research (clinical research and innovation)|Strengthen international patient footprint via Patient Assistance Centres to support medical value travel demand|The Board recommended a final dividend of Rs.2 per equity share (20% of the Rs.10 face value) for FY2025-26, subject to shareholder approval at the 25th AGM. The Company maintains a formal Dividend Distribution Policy (named among its key governance policies), though its detailed payout philosophy is not elaborated within this text bundle.
currentContext.expansion: Capacity expansion is central to Max Healthcare's growth strategy, pursued through a balanced mix of brownfield, greenfield and asset-light initiatives. During FY2025-26 the Company commissioned/operationalised brownfield towers at Max Super Speciality Hospital, Mohali (160 beds, taking capacity from 220 to a materially higher base, ~73% increase), at Nanavati-Max Super Speciality Hospital, Mumbai (280-bed Phase-I tower, services live since December 2025, with Phase-II of 271 beds scheduled to start on-ground construction in FY2026-27), and at Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital, Saket, Delhi (400-bed tower, 156 beds already handed over, balance to be operationalised in due course, services live from April 2026). At Max Super Speciality Hospital, Dwarka (a 303-bed hospital operated under an O&M agreement with Muthoot Hospitals Private Limited since July 2024), the Board approved (February 5, 2026) extending the arrangement to add ~260 further beds at the same site. At Max Super Speciality Hospital, Nagpur (run via wholly-owned subsidiary Alexis Multi-Speciality Hospital Private Limited), the Board approved (May 20, 2025) adding ~100 beds to the existing 200-bed facility by constructing two additional floors, to be completed over the next 2-3 years. A ~1-acre land parcel adjoining Max Super Speciality Hospital, Vaishali was acquired (May 16, 2025) for ~Rs.120 Crore, expected to enable ~200 additional beds over the next 2-3 years. A long-term lease was signed for a new 130-bed built-to-suit hospital near the existing 223-bed Max Dehradun, focused on advanced oncology/radiation therapy, with ~Rs.170-200 Crore of Company investment (biomedical equipment, furniture etc., funded via internal accruals) and commissioning expected by FY2028-29. In Pune, the Company executed a share purchase agreement (Board approved December 18, 2025) for staggered acquisition of 100% of Yerawada Properties Private Limited to develop a ~450-bed super-speciality hospital at an estimated total project cost of ~Rs.1,020 Crore, targeted for commissioning within about four years (by FY2029-30), marking its fourth facility in Western India. In Lucknow, the Board approved (May 21, 2026) construction of Phase-I of a new Max Super Speciality Hospital on the Company's 5-acre Shaheed Path land parcel, with ~712 census beds and total construction & equipment cost of ~Rs.1,400 Crore (blended cost per bed ~Rs.1.97 Crore, excluding land), to address an existing Lucknow network hospital operating at peak occupancy. In Bhubaneswar, the Company acquired a ~58.28% controlling stake (May 18, 2026) in Kalinga Hospital Ltd, a 250-bed NABH-accredited multi-speciality facility on a 10-acre central campus, for an equity value of ~Rs.297.97 Crore, marking entry into Eastern India with brownfield headroom to scale the site beyond 1,000 beds over time. Taken together, management describes the overall pipeline as having the potential to add over 8,300 beds, including approximately 4,000 beds over the next three to four years. Inorganic growth is pursued with a disciplined acquisition approach targeting ROCE of 20-25% within four years of acquisition; recent acquisitions in Noida, Lucknow and Nagpur are being integrated with improving utilisation and case mix, and are seen as offering further brownfield expansion potential.

risks.risk: High-risk litigation, fire incidents or significant regulatory changes
risks.note: Management explicitly flags that while no single risk currently presents an existential concern, events such as high-risk litigations, fire incidents, or significant regulatory changes could materially affect operations and reputation if not managed effectively — relevant given the hospital network's scale and safety-critical operating environment.

risks.risk: Integration and ramp-up risk from acquired hospitals
risks.note: The Company is exposed to risks associated with the integration and operational ramp-up of newly acquired hospitals, relevant given its active inorganic growth strategy (e.g., Noida, Lucknow, Nagpur integrations, and further acquisitions such as Kalinga Hospital).

risks.risk: Cyber security and data privacy exposure
risks.note: As the Company's digital footprint expands (digital health platforms, AI tools, electronic health records), cyber security and data privacy have emerged as critical focus areas, reinforcing the need for robust IT governance and strict regulatory adherence.

risks.risk: Rising leverage tied to expansion funding
risks.note: Finance costs rose primarily due to higher borrowings undertaken to fund completed and ongoing capacity expansion projects at Mohali, Mumbai and Gurugram, plus the full-year impact of borrowings related to the Jaypee Healthcare acquisition; the Debt Service Coverage Ratio declined year-on-year, with the change attributed to increased borrowings for expansion projects.

The Company's enterprise risk register grew to 68 risks as at March 31, 2026 (three new risks added during FY2025-26) spanning operational, regulatory, medical, strategic, IT, financial, legal/compliance and human-resource domains, reflecting an increasingly complex risk landscape as the network scales.

The Company's risk management framework spans operational, legal, treasury, human resource, taxation, regulatory, strategic and financial domains, indicating that regulatory/compliance risk is a structural feature of operating a large, integrated, multi-state healthcare network.

one-line thesis: Max Healthcare delivered steady 10% revenue growth in Q4FY26 driven by volume (OBDs +8%), but faced a structural margin headwind from discontinuing low-margin institutional oncology drugs (-5% oncology share). The strategic pivot involves absorbing this permanent revenue mix shift while aggressively ramping 20% new brownfield capacity and entering Eastern India via the profitable Kalinga acquisition, positioning FY27 for operating leverage as new beds fill.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 2,664cr (+10% YoY, +2% QoQ); EBITDA: INR 682cr (+8% YoY), Margin 26.8% (-40bps YoY) due to oncology drug discontinuation and higher ALOS; PAT: INR 387cr (+3% YoY); Order Book: N/A (Service sector); Net Debt: INR 1,908cr (Net Debt/EBITDA <1x). One-offs: Discontinuation of high-value chemo drugs for institutional patients reduced oncology revenue share to 21% (from 26% YoY), impacting top-line by ~INR 50cr quarterly run-rate; ALOS temporarily up 9% due to phased bed commissioning.
guidance: Revenue Growth: Mid-to-high single digits organic + capacity additions; Margin: Expect recovery as new beds ramp (operating leverage), oncology share to stabilize at 21-22%; Order Inflow: Strong demand in Lucknow/Delhi NCR; Capex: INR 1,400cr approved for Lucknow greenfield; Commissioning: Gurgaon (500 beds) by end-FY27, Mohali/Nagpur by FY28.
order book & pipeline: Expansion Pipeline: 500 beds Gurgaon (FY27); 700 beds Lucknow Greenfield (Board approved INR 1,400cr); 400 beds Mohali (FY28); 260 beds Dwarka (24 months); 200 beds Vaishali (pending approval); 400 beds Patparganj (FY29). Total upcoming capacity ~2,500+ beds over 3-4 years.
segment / subsidiary detail: Hospitals: 75%+ occupancy, ARPOB INR 77,900; Oncology share dropped to 21% (vs 26% YoY) due to CGHS drug pricing policy; International Patients: INR 227cr (+12% YoY, 9% of hospital rev); Max@Home: INR 73cr (+30% YoY); Max Lab: INR 52cr (+14% YoY). Digital revenue 31% of total.
growth verticals / optionality: Eastern India entry via Kalinga Hospital (Bhubaneswar, 250 beds, already profitable); Lucknow cluster strategy (Gomti Nagar expansion + 700-bed Shaheed Path greenfield); Phased brownfield ramp-up in Delhi/Mumbai/Punjab yielding operating leverage as occupancy stabilizes near 80%.
margins & cost dynamics: EBITDA margin compressed 40bps YoY to 26.8% primarily due to exit of low-margin (16%) but high-revenue oncology drugs for institutional patients; Doctor costs elevated due to pre-hiring for new capacities (INR 435cr in Q4), expected to normalize with operating leverage; CGHS rate revision benefit (INR 140cr annualized net) partially offset drug loss, with INR 30-40cr yet to flow.
capex / expansion: INR 328cr deployed in Q4 for expansion/upgrades; FY26 total capex INR 1,627cr + INR 131cr land purchase; Major upcoming: INR 1,400cr for Lucknow greenfield; Gurgaon interior/facade works ongoing.
capital allocation: Debt reduction priority (Net debt down to INR 1,908cr from INR 2,166cr); Dividend paid INR 146cr in FY26; M&A active (Kalinga Hospital acquisition); Reinvestment in brownfield/greenfield projects to capture market share in North/East India.
risks & watch-items: Regulatory Pricing: CGHS/ECHS mandate for 30% discount on chemo drugs causing permanent revenue mix shift and potential patient attrition to unorganized sector; Execution Risk: Delays in Gurgaon/Lucknow commissioning due to labor shortages (LPG crisis/elections); Talent Inflation: Rising doctor costs in competitive micro-markets; ALOS Volatility: Temporary inefficiencies during phased bed rollouts.
management quality / tone: Confident on volume growth and capacity utilization; Pragmatic on oncology drug issue (viewed as permanent structural shift, not temporary); Aggressive on expansion (Lucknow/Gurgaon) despite macro headwinds; Emphasized 'cluster approach' to mitigate doctor talent bottlenecks.
non-obvious takeaways: Oncology drug discontinuation is industry-wide but impacts Max disproportionately due to high institutional mix; Management views the exit of these drugs as margin-accretive long-term despite top-line hit (exiting 'perverse' margins); Kalinga Hospital was acquired profitably (INR 10cr annual EBITDA), avoiding typical startup losses; ALOS increase is a tactical artifact of opening beds only when demand exists, not clinical inefficiency.

| Rising doctor talent costs and competition for specialists in saturated micro-markets. | Apollo Hospitals Enterprise Ltd | beneficiary | Low | Large peers with diversified geography may absorb talent cost inflation better, though Max's cluster strategy mitigates this specific risk. |

themes.title: Hospitals, diagnostics & domestic healthcare
themes.need: Under-bedded India plus insurance penetration and preventive-care adoption drive a domestic healthcare capex + volume cycle distinct from export pharma. MAXHEALTH adding ~2,500+ beds (Gurgaon 500-bed by FY27); APOLLOHOSP/MEDANTA/KIMS/NH/ASTERDM/MAXHEALTH on hospitals; LALPATHLAB/METROPOLIS/THYROCARE/VIJAYA on diagnostics (LALPATHLAB guides 13-15% FY27); MEDPLUS/ENTERO on pharmacy/distribution; POLYMED on devices. The same India-only demand engine now also carries India-facing branded pharma, which is driven by domestic volume and price rather than the export book: GLAXO delivered its first INR 1,000cr quarter with 8.1% revenue growth, Shingrix at a ~INR 75cr annual run-rate (CY25, +80% YoY) and Jemperli's first-line approval expanding eligible patients from 800 to 6,000; ERIS (dermatology 15% of revenue after INR 1,265cr of domestic brand acquisitions), SANOFI (India-for-India, NLEM price cuts) and THEMISMED (hospital segment +20% YoY) sit on the same axis.
themes.driver: New-bed commissioning + occupancy ramp; Tier 3/4 diagnostics penetration; CGHS rate revision; preventive-test volumes; domestic branded-formulation volume growth and NLEM/price actions.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Max Healthcare Institute Limited operates a network of 21 healthcare facilities across 11 cities in India with over 6,000 beds, delivering tertiary and quaternary care across specialities including oncology, cardiac sciences, neurosciences, orthopaedics, renal sciences and organ transplantation. Beyond hospitals, the Company extends its care ecosystem through Max Lab (pathology and diagnostics) and Max@Home (home healthcare and wellness services), and serves international patients through Patient Assistance Centres across multiple countries.

order_book.title: Order book & pipeline
order_book.body: Expansion Pipeline: 500 beds Gurgaon (FY27); 700 beds Lucknow Greenfield (Board approved INR 1,400cr); 400 beds Mohali (FY28); 260 beds Dwarka (24 months); 200 beds Vaishali (pending approval); 400 beds Patparganj (FY29). Total upcoming capacity ~2,500+ beds over 3-4 years.

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.body: Revenue Growth: Mid-to-high single digits organic + capacity additions; Margin: Expect recovery as new beds ramp (operating leverage), oncology share to stabilize at 21-22%; Order Inflow: Strong demand in Lucknow/Delhi NCR; Capex: INR 1,400cr approved for Lucknow greenfield; Commissioning: Gurgaon (500 beds) by end-FY27, Mohali/Nagpur by FY28.

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body: Eastern India entry via Kalinga Hospital (Bhubaneswar, 250 beds, already profitable); Lucknow cluster strategy (Gomti Nagar expansion + 700-bed Shaheed Path greenfield); Phased brownfield ramp-up in Delhi/Mumbai/Punjab yielding operating leverage as occupancy stabilizes near 80%.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Structural demand driven by demographic shifts (rising share of population aged 60+ and 40-59), rising disease complexity and greater health awareness, shifting demand towards organised, high-quality care
- Healthcare infrastructure gap — India at ~16 hospital beds per 10,000 population versus a global average of 33 — is a key long-term structural growth driver supporting sustained capacity expansion
- Transition from episodic hospital-based treatment to integrated, lifecycle-based continuum-of-care (diagnostics, homecare, rehabilitation, preventive services) is opening additional revenue streams beyond inpatient care
- Rising health insurance coverage (from ~35% in FY19 to ~41% in FY25, projected to reach 45-50% by FY26) is improving affordability, increasing hospitalisation rates and driving demand for elective/planned procedures, alongside a shift towards institutional/insurer contracts
- Medical tourism remains a structural opportunity for India (10th in Medical Tourism Index) though demand has seen a slight recent moderation due to a decline in medical visas from certain geographies
- Favourable government policy support — Union Budget 2026-27 raised Ministry of Health and Family Welfare allocation by 10% to Rs.1,06,530 crore and National Health Mission allocation to Rs.39,390 crore, including a scheme to establish five Regional Medical Hubs with the private sector
- Gradual consolidation of the fragmented Indian hospital market (organised players ~30% share) via capacity additions, acquisitions and asset-light models is expected to strengthen organised providers and standardisation of care
- Technology adoption (AI-enabled diagnostics, robotics, data-driven decision-making) is cited as a strategic differentiator enhancing clinical precision, outcomes and operational efficiency
- Overall expansion pipeline has the potential to add over 8,300 beds, including approximately 4,000 beds over the next three to four years
- Mumbai (Nanavati-Max): 280-bed brownfield tower largely commissioned and partially operationalised, with strong ramp-up; Phase II (271 additional beds) on-ground work expected to commence upon full commissioning of Phase I
- Mohali: 160-bed brownfield tower operationalised (+70% capacity), witnessing healthy ramp-up; a 400-bed asset-light hospital is being planned in Zirakpur (Tricity region)
- Saket, Delhi (Max Smart): 400-bed brownfield tower being operationalised in phases — 156 beds already handed over, balance expected to be commissioned over the next quarter
- Dwarka, Delhi: 303-bed hospital commissioned under the Company's first asset-light greenfield model; a further 260-bed brownfield tower is planned
- Lucknow: capacity being augmented to approximately 570 beds at the existing facility, plus a planned 712-bed greenfield hospital on a 5-acre land parcel at Shaheed Path
- Bhubaneswar: 58.28% controlling stake acquired in Kalinga Hospital Ltd, a 250-bed NABH-accredited multi-speciality facility on a ~10-acre land parcel

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: EBITDA margin compressed 40bps YoY to 26.8% primarily due to exit of low-margin (16%) but high-revenue oncology drugs for institutional patients; Doctor costs elevated due to pre-hiring for new capacities (INR 435cr in Q4), expected to normalize with operating leverage; CGHS rate revision benefit (INR 140cr annualized net) partially offset drug loss, with INR 30-40cr yet to flow.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Debt reduction priority (Net debt down to INR 1,908cr from INR 2,166cr); Dividend paid INR 146cr in FY26; M&A active (Kalinga Hospital acquisition); Reinvestment in brownfield/greenfield projects to capture market share in North/East India.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Capacity expansion is central to Max Healthcare's growth strategy, pursued through a balanced mix of brownfield, greenfield and asset-light initiatives. During FY2025-26 the Company commissioned/operationalised brownfield towers at Max Super Speciality Hospital, Mohali (160 beds, taking capacity from 220 to a materially higher base, ~73% increase), at Nanavati-Max Super Speciality Hospital, Mumbai (280-bed Phase-I tower, services live since December 2025, with Phase-II of 271 beds scheduled to start on-ground construction in FY2026-27), and at Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital, Saket, Delhi (400-bed tower, 156 beds already handed over, balance to be operationalised in due course, services live from April 2026). At Max Super Speciality Hospital, Dwarka (a 303-bed hospital operated under an O&M agreement with Muthoot Hospitals Private Limited since July 2024), the Board approved (February 5, 2026) extending the arrangement to add ~260 further beds at the same site. At Max Super Speciality Hospital, Nagpur (run via wholly-owned subsidiary Alexis Multi-Speciality Hospital Private Limited), the Board approved (May 20, 2025) adding ~100 beds to the existing 200-bed facility by constructing two additional floors, to be completed over the next 2-3 years. A ~1-acre land parcel adjoining Max Super Speciality Hospital, Vaishali was acquired (May 16, 2025) for ~Rs.120 Crore, expected to enable ~200 additional beds over the next 2-3 years. A long-term lease was signed for a new 130-bed built-to-suit hospital near the existing 223-bed Max Dehradun, focused on advanced oncology/radiation therapy, with ~Rs.170-200 Crore of Company investment (biomedical equipment, furniture etc., funded via internal accruals) and commissioning expected by FY2028-29. In Pune, the Company executed a share purchase agreement (Board approved December 18, 2025) for staggered acquisition of 100% of Yerawada Properties Private Limited to develop a ~450-bed super-speciality hospital at an estimated total project cost of ~Rs.1,020 Crore, targeted for commissioning within about four years (by FY2029-30), marking its fourth facility in Western India. In Lucknow, the Board approved (May 21, 2026) construction of Phase-I of a new Max Super Speciality Hospital on the Company's 5-acre Shaheed Path land parcel, with ~712 census beds and total construction & equipment cost of ~Rs.1,400 Crore (blended cost per bed ~Rs.1.97 Crore, excluding land), to address an existing Lucknow network hospital operating at peak occupancy. In Bhubaneswar, the Company acquired a ~58.28% controlling stake (May 18, 2026) in Kalinga Hospital Ltd, a 250-bed NABH-accredited multi-speciality facility on a 10-acre central campus, for an equity value of ~Rs.297.97 Crore, marking entry into Eastern India with brownfield headroom to scale the site beyond 1,000 beds over time. Taken together, management describes the overall pipeline as having the potential to add over 8,300 beds, including approximately 4,000 beds over the next three to four years. Inorganic growth is pursued with a disciplined acquisition approach targeting ROCE of 20-25% within four years of acquisition; recent acquisitions in Noida, Lucknow and Nagpur are being integrated with improving utilisation and case mix, and are seen as offering further brownfield expansion potential.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident on volume growth and capacity utilization; Pragmatic on oncology drug issue (viewed as permanent structural shift, not temporary); Aggressive on expansion (Lucknow/Gurgaon) despite macro headwinds; Emphasized 'cluster approach' to mitigate doctor talent bottlenecks.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Scale as India's most valuable listed healthcare organisation, with an integrated network of 21 facilities and 6,000+ beds across 11 cities
- High network utilisation — 76% occupancy in FY2025-26, with ~73% of beds located in metro markets
- Asset-light, scalable growth model combining owned/operated hospitals, subsidiaries, managed facilities and Partner Healthcare Facilities (PHFs)
- Advanced clinical technology base — 42 robotic surgical systems (including Da Vinci platforms) and the EDGE radiosurgery system, supporting complex, high-acuity procedures
- International patient network via 12 Patient Assistance Centres across multiple countries plus 5 partner offices, supporting medical value travel demand
- Governance recognition — IiAS 'Next Leader' for the second consecutive year (top 20 in S&P BSE100 for corporate governance) and inclusion in the NIFTY 50 Index
- Growing AI/digital capability built on a multimodal longitudinal electronic health data repository, applied across the patient journey (symptom search, pre-OPD assessment, discharge summary optimisation, health-record analysis)

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Regulatory Pricing: CGHS/ECHS mandate for 30% discount on chemo drugs causing permanent revenue mix shift and potential patient attrition to unorganized sector; Execution Risk: Delays in Gurgaon/Lucknow commissioning due to labor shortages (LPG crisis/elections); Talent Inflation: Rising doctor costs in competitive micro-markets; ALOS Volatility: Temporary inefficiencies during phased bed rollouts.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Oncology drug discontinuation is industry-wide but impacts Max disproportionately due to high institutional mix; Management views the exit of these drugs as margin-accretive long-term despite top-line hit (exiting 'perverse' margins); Kalinga Hospital was acquired profitably (INR 10cr annual EBITDA), avoiding typical startup losses; ALOS increase is a tactical artifact of opening beds only when demand exists, not clinical inefficiency.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Multi-pronged growth approach: expanding capacity organically, scaling through asset-light models, and pursuing disciplined inorganic growth initiatives
- Capital allocation framework emphasising disciplined growth, balance sheet prudence and return-accretive deployment of capital; intends to maintain net debt-to-EBITDA at not more than 2.5x
- Prioritise high-return brownfield expansions and asset-light opportunities, while selectively pursuing greenfield projects in attractive catchments with compelling demand fundamentals and clinical talent availability
